title: Interface-Aware Smoke Tests and Deterministic Import Autofix for Feature-Level Coding Agents: A Negative Result

contributions.purpose: Automates repair of import and name resolution errors (NameError, ImportError, AttributeError) that coding agents hit during feature development.
contributions.mechanism: Interface-aware smoke tests derived from the task's interface specification run after each code edit; on target-class failures the system searches for candidate definitions and deterministically inserts the missing import when exactly one unambiguous candidate exists.
contributions.evaluation: Evaluated on FeatureBench Lite (30 tasks); the autofix mechanism achieves the same 10.0% resolved rate as baseline.
contributions.domain: LLM coding agents / automated program repair
contributions.source_quote: We propose interface-aware smoke tests with deterministic import autofix for coding agents, targeting a common class of runtime errors.

contributions.purpose: Isolates the individual effects of diagnostic feedback versus automated fixes in agent scaffolds.
contributions.mechanism: A three-condition controlled experiment: baseline (no intervention), diagnose-only (diagnostic reports without code changes), and full autofix (diagnostics plus automated fixes).
contributions.evaluation: Conducted on FeatureBench Lite (30 tasks); diagnose-only achieves 16.67% resolved rate vs 10.0% for baseline and full autofix.
contributions.source_quote: We conduct a rigorous three-condition experiment on FeatureBench Lite (30 tasks) that isolates the effects of diagnostic feedback and automated fixes.

contributions.purpose: Reports that deterministic autofix provides no benefit for feature-level coding tasks.
contributions.mechanism: Comparison of full-autofix condition against baseline, plus two optimization iterations of the autofix pipeline.
contributions.evaluation: Autofix matches baseline at 10.0% resolved rate (no benefit), and two optimization iterations degraded performance.
contributions.source_quote: We report a negative result: deterministic autofix provides no benefit over baseline, while two optimization iterations degraded performance.

contributions.purpose: Explains the null effect of the autofix intervention.
contributions.mechanism: Workflow analysis quantifying how often the target error class occurs in agent trajectories.
contributions.evaluation: The target error class accounts for only ~4-5% of agent workflow, too rare to impact overall performance.
contributions.source_quote: We provide analysis showing the target error class is too rare (~4-5% of workflow) to impact overall performance.

contributions.purpose: Shows that diagnostic feedback alone helps agents more than automated fixing.
contributions.mechanism: Comparison of the diagnose-only condition (diagnostic reports without code changes) against baseline and full autofix.
contributions.evaluation: Diagnose-only improves resolved rate by 66.7% relative (16.67% vs 10.0%), suggesting agents benefit from understanding errors rather than having them fixed automatically.
contributions.source_quote: We find that diagnostic feedback alone improves performance by 66.7%, suggesting agents benefit from understanding errors rather than having them fixed automatically.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Our work extends APR concepts to agent workflows by proposing deterministic fixes for import and name resolution errors, though our results suggest this approach has limited applicability for feature-level tasks.
These approaches rely on agents interpreting error messages and self-correcting, which motivates our investigation of whether automated fixes can reduce this cognitive burden.

notes: Explicit negative-result paper (stated in title). Autofix ties baseline (10.0% vs 10.0%), optimization iterations degraded performance; only the diagnose-only ablation improved results. Paper carries an automated-research-system generation warning.
